vignette:
Sarah came to the clinic because she believed she was about to lose her job, the last piece of structured normalcy she felt she had. At twenty-five, she had been driving city buses for nearly two years, a job she took after her honorable discharge. The massive vehicle, the prescribed route, the sense of responsibility—it had all felt like a manageable civilian echo of her role as a driver in a military transport unit. For a time, it was. But the incident that had ended her tour of duty had followed her home, and now it sat with her in the driver’s seat every single day. The memory was not a constant film, but a series of sensory fragments, jagged and sharp. It was the sudden, oppressive silence just before the blast, the way the dust tasted like metal, and most of all, the sickening, weightless lurch as the vehicle was thrown. The world had spun, a nauseating kaleidoscope of sky and sand, and in that moment of profound disorientation, she had been certain she was dying.

Now, any hint of that physical sensation sends a jolt of pure terror through her. A simple dizzy spell, the kind that comes from standing up too fast, is no longer benign. When it happens, the fluorescent lights of the bus depot restroom seem to warp, her breath catches high in her chest, and the tiled floor feels as unstable as the Iraqi desert. She has to brace herself against the wall, her heart hammering against her ribs, convinced the world is about to violently upend itself again. This physical reactivity has become a central and terrifying feature of her life. The unpredictability of her own body feels like the most intimate betrayal. Because of this, she began calling in sick on days she woke up feeling even slightly lightheaded, a pattern her supervisor had started to notice.

Her work environment, once a source of comfort, has transformed into a landscape of potential threats. Sarah drives with a vigilance that goes far beyond professional caution. Her eyes don't just scan for traffic; they flick constantly to parked cars, to overpasses, to debris on the roadside, her mind cataloging anomalies and potential dangers. She finds herself scrutinizing the passengers in her rearview mirror, her body tensing when someone boards too quickly or carries a bulky backpack. She has come to believe that disaster is always imminent, and that only her constant watchfulness keeps it at bay. In public spaces, this need for control is absolute. In the depot breakroom, she will stand if it means avoiding a chair that doesn't have its back to a solid wall. The thought of someone approaching her from behind is intolerable; she must be able to see every entrance, every person, every potential variable.

Over the past year, these behaviors have calcified, shrinking her world until only the rigid lines of her bus route and the four walls of her apartment remain. She has stopped seeing the few friends she kept in touch with from the service. The easy camaraderie they once shared now feels fraught with the peril of unpredictable conversations and spontaneous plans. Inside this self-imposed isolation, a set of bleak convictions has taken root. She looks at her life and sees only wreckage. The competent, trusted soldier she once was feels like a stranger. How could that person be the same woman who now trembles at the thought of a traffic detour? She is certain her life has been destroyed by the trauma, that the person she was meant to be is gone forever. Nothing feels meaningful anymore; the days are just something to be survived, a series of threats to be monitored and navigated until she can retreat to the safety of her home. It was after a particularly bad dizzy spell on a crowded afternoon route—one that forced her to pull over, gripping the wheel to stop her hands from shaking—that she finally made the call. The fear of causing an accident, of failing in this one last role she felt capable of, was finally greater than the fear of facing the memory itself.
